body.heading: Catching moving air
paragraphs: Sound is vibration travelling through the air in waves of squeezing and stretching. Your outer ear is a funnel shaped to catch those waves and guide them down the ear canal to the eardrum, a taut sheet of skin no wider than a fingernail.
When sound waves arrive, the eardrum vibrates in step with them — fast for high notes, slow for low ones. That vibration is still far too weak to work with directly, so the middle ear amplifies it.

body.heading: Three tiny bones and a snail
paragraphs: Behind the eardrum sit the ossicles, the three smallest bones in the body — the hammer, anvil and stirrup. Acting as a chain of levers, they pass the eardrum's movement to a much smaller window, concentrating the force so it can move fluid. The stirrup, the last of the three, is only about three millimetres long — smaller than a grain of rice.

Beyond that window lies the cochlea, a coiled tube shaped like a snail shell and filled with fluid. The vibration sets the fluid moving, and thousands of hair cells lining the tube bend as it passes, each responding best to a particular pitch.

body.heading: From bending hairs to hearing
paragraphs: When a hair cell bends, it fires an electrical signal along the auditory nerve to the brain, which reads the pattern — which hairs, how fast they fire — as pitch and volume. Loudness is measured in the size of the vibration, pitch in its speed.
The system is delicate. Very loud sounds can flatten hair cells permanently, and unlike many body cells they do not grow back — the reason hearing damage from noise is cumulative and irreversible.

takeaway: The eardrum and three tiny bones pass sound vibrations to the cochlea, where hair cells convert them into nerve signals the brain hears as sound.
